title: ‘A dream come true’: showjumper on course for history after Rolex Grand Prix victory
content:
The stadium at CHIO Aachen is the cathedral of showjumping and 40,000 spectators descended there on Sunday to worship at its altar, witnessing the best Rolex Grand Prix held there since statistical records began in 2010.

The horses and riders who lined up to contest the €500,000 (US$580,200) first prize were in the form of their lives, all wishing for their names to be etched on the wall among the pantheon of greats who have come before them.

After two days of fierce qualifying rounds, 40 competitors came forward for Sunday’s thriller, which was held over three rounds, with the 18 best progressing from round one into round two. Whoever jumped clear in the first two rounds progressed to the jump-off against the clock.

Just three riders managed this, and it was Germany’s Richard Vogel, ranked third in the world, who walked away with the honour of being the 2026 Aachen Rolex Grand Prix champion.

Riding the 14-year-old stallion United Touch S, with whom he became European Champion last year, Vogel put in three rounds of immaculate jumping.

The bay, who is known for his massive stride and gravity-defying scope, is owned and bred by Julius-Peter Sinnack, and ate up the Aachen turf smoothly. The pair stopped the clock in the jump-off on 45.57 seconds, some 1.79 seconds ahead of second-placed Argentinian combination Jose Maria Larocca Jr and Finn Lente.

“It’s a dream come true to win this class,” said Vogel. “This is my favourite show in the world – winning it is something incredible and for sure, we will never forget this day.”

The Aachen Rolex Grand Prix forms 25 per cent of the Rolex Grand Slam of Showjumping, which can only be won if a rider wins three consecutive majors. Vogel came into this competition as a live contender for the Grand Slam, having won the Dutch Masters aboard United Touch S in March, earning him a bonus €500,000 for this second consecutive win. He could net a further €1million in bonuses if he wins at Spruce Meadows.

“But it’s a real childhood dream come true to achieve it with such a special horse,” said Vogel. “The whole team who take care of United Touch deserve this too – it’s so special and we’re just thrilled how well he performed today.”

Vogel has very carefully plotted United Touch’s 2026 campaign and Aachen marked just the third show of the year for the stallion. That might, on paper, seem a surprisingly light schedule for a horse of this calibre, but the pair arrived here on sensational form having won the World Cup in Basel and the Dutch Masters.

“Coming here as a live contender is a nice pressure to have – it’s a real privilege,” added Vogel. “The luck was on our side, for sure. But as my grandpa always said, ‘no one ever won with bad luck’, so we’ll take it.”

Vogel was second of the three riders to go in the jump-off, with his partner, fellow German Sophie Hinners, the first to take on the third and final round. Riding Iron Dames Singclair, who has jumped clear in all of his Major starts, Hinners posted an immaculate clear in a time of 51.62 seconds in a bid to become just the second female rider in history to win this grand prix after the USA’s Beezie Madden in 2019. Hinners ultimately had to settle for third, taking home €225,000.

Larocca Jr and Finn Lente, who were billed as underdogs in this competition, were the last to go in the jump-off but ultimately finished second, winning €300,000. Though the win eluded them, Larocca Jr nevertheless carved out a small space in Argentinian showjumping history: no rider from the country had ever finished on a Masters podium before.

One million euros richer, Vogel will doubtless be considering the possibility of a flight to Canada in September for leg three of the Rolex Grand Slam in Spruce Meadows. But in a championship year, chasing personal goals – and major paydays – isn’t quite as straightforward as it might otherwise be.

Spruce Meadows falls just a month after August’s World Championships, to be held at Aachen, and with Vogel a hot favourite for German team selection, questions abound about whether he’ll choose one opportunity, the other, or take the risk of trying for both.

If he does cross the Atlantic, he’ll do so in pursuit of a title that only one rider has previously claimed, some 11 years ago. In any case, as he makes the short three-hour journey home to Marburg, the dream remains very much alive for Vogel and his marriage of success with United Touch.

Gemma Redrup
